newsitem.title: USA: Clinton to dine with governors Sunday, meet Monday.
newsitem.headline: Clinton to dine with governors Sunday, meet Monday.

text.p: President Clinton will host state governors at a White House dinner on Sunday night, allowing him to socialize with his former colleagues before they hold a Monday morning meeting that may prove contentious.

Clinton, who was governor of Arkansas until he was elected president in 1992, has long-standing ties to many governors as well as a genuine interest in the nuts-and-bolts policy issues that dominate their working days.
On Monday, he was to hold a roundtable with them at 9:15 a.m. EST which the White House said was likely to cover issues ranging from welfare reform to the Medicare and Medicaid health care programs.
On many of these matters, Clinton and the governors do not see eye to eye.

The governors, who began a four-day Washington meeting of the National Governors Association Saturday, have said they will oppose any Clinton plan to cap funding for the Medicaid health care program for 37 million poor, elderly and disabled.
"All of us are joined at the hip and opposed to the caps," Ohio Republican Gov. George Voinovich said Saturday.
On Sunday, White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles told reporters the White House was committed to imposing spending limits on Medicaid despite opposition from governors.

Clinton and Republican governors also disagree on his plan to revisit last year's welfare reform law that ended the 61-year federal guarantee of aid to the poor and gave the states broad power to design their own welfare programs.

On Saturday, Republican governors voted to oppose a draft NGA policy statement asking Congress to restore benefits to some legal immigrants who will lose Food Stamps and federal disability aid under the law.

Clinton administration officials, supported by many state governors with large immigrant populations, have said they plan to ask Congress to restore more than $16 billion in spending cuts under the law to restore such benefits.
Bowles Sunday shrugged off the opposition by the Republican governors to reopening the law. "We're not going to be able to agree on all things at all times," he said.
